Case-content proposal for m00003. The brief supplies no concrete inventory, timetable or individual participant requirements. The following is a proposed fictional starting fixture, not an observation about a real workshop or an approval of an implementation. All operating rules below apply only to this invented case.

Proposed scenario data:
{
  "title": "Welcome cards in Harbor Room",
  "facts": [
    "The activity runs from 14:00 to 14:30 for four confirmed participants. Each participant is to leave with one welcome card.",
    "The room has one shared table with four seats, eight blank cards, four sets of markers, four ready-to-use printed welcome captions and four copies of the activity instructions in large print. These resources are available for the whole session. The printed captions can be used directly without cutting or adhesive.",
    "One shared label printer is available from 14:00 until 14:15. It has supplies for four labels. Four welcome-caption jobs are already prepared; each job takes two minutes, including setup, and jobs run one at a time.",
    "Bea, the designated printer assistant, is available from 14:00 until 14:10. The workshop volunteer can guide the manual card activity.",
    "Ada has requested large-print instructions. Ivo has requested a seated activity. No other participant needs or preferences have been supplied.",
    "The organizer has mentioned a possible fifth participant but has not confirmed their attendance or supplied their requirements."
  ],
  "constraints": [
    "In this fictional workshop, Bea must operate the printer throughout every print job; the volunteer and participants may not operate it alone.",
    "Return shared equipment by the end of its availability. Do not assume additional supplies, seats, assistance or time.",
    "A card may use a printed label, a ready-to-use caption, or marker decoration. Printer use is optional.",
    "Provide the requested large-print instructions and a seated way to take part. Do not infer additional participant needs.",
    "Plan for the four confirmed participants. Clarify attendance and resource needs before extending the plan to a fifth person."
  ],
  "task": "Propose an activity plan for the four confirmed participants. Explain which supplied facts support your choices of resources, timing, assistance and participant support. Give a fallback if the printer or its required assistance becomes unavailable, and identify anything you need clarified."
}

A plausible initial plan: offer the four seated places and the large-print instructions, with blank cards and markers available at the table. If the four prepared print jobs are wanted, Bea can operate them sequentially from 14:00 to 14:08; four jobs at two minutes each fit both Bea's availability and the printer reservation and use exactly the four available labels. Participants can choose a printed label, a ready-to-use caption or marker decoration for their card; these are options, not inferred preferences. Return the printer within its reservation and use the remaining session for the card activity. This plan meets the stated inventory, scheduling and support constraints. The facts do not establish how quickly each participant will complete the activity or whether each will prefer printing, so do not promise either. A wholly manual plan is also consistent with the case; the printer plan is not the sole acceptable choice.

Proposed changed condition: replace the Bea-availability fact with 'Bea is unavailable for the entire 14:00–14:30 session; no replacement printer assistant is available.' Retain the other facts and constraints. The printer may still be physically available, but no printer-based plan is supported because its mandatory operator is absent. A reasoned fallback is to offer the four existing captions, blank cards and markers at the seated table with the large-print instructions. This uses supplies already listed and preserves the stated participant provisions. Do not silently relax the printer rule or invent another assistant. If a new requirement makes printed labels essential, clarification or a changed activity agreement is needed; the current case does not contain that requirement.

The unresolved attendance issue warrants a concrete clarification: will a fifth participant attend, and if so what additional seating, instructions and participant requirements are confirmed? Eight blank cards alone do not establish capacity for five. Continue the bounded plan for four while that request remains unresolved.

Content limits for replacement cases: these people, timings, permissions, supplies and example plans belong only to this fixture. A replacement scenario may describe entirely different resources and constraints; missing facts must remain unknown, and contradictory facts warrant clarification. Do not carry this example's permission for manual alternatives or its printer rule into unrelated user content. Learning Sciences and Assessment should determine the teaching and evidence strategy; Software Engineering should determine how to implement the required editable scenario and state controls. Those are dependencies outside my assigned remit. No implemented version exists for me to review or approve.

Learning-design proposal answering m00003. No implementation or learner evidence exists yet, so this is a proposed instructional design, not approval or a claim that learning has occurred. The concrete workshop facts and operating permissions come from Subject-Matter Expertise's proposed fixture in m00005. The learning design should also work when the user replaces that fixture.

Observable capability: given a supplied fictional case, the learner can propose a plan, explain how its material resource, timing, assistance and participant-support choices follow from the stated facts and constraints, identify an uncertainty that requires clarification, and adapt the plan when a relevant condition changes. When the original activity cannot be supported, the learner should justify an available alternative or a request for clarification. The target is the connection between evidence and action, including recognizing what is unknown; a particular preferred activity is not the target. Feasibility judgments about the workshop itself remain within Subject-Matter Expertise's remit.

Distinguish three levels of performance. Recognition is identifying a listed constraint or choosing an offered alternative; it can orient the learner but does not demonstrate plan construction. Supported production is writing and revising a plan with the facts, reasoning prompts, feedback or examples available; this is the main practice proposed here. Independent transfer would require constructing and justifying a plan in a meaningfully different supplied case without answer-specific hints, the previous model plan or corrective feedback before submission. The case facts should remain available, because the target is using facts rather than memorizing the inventory. Success in this same-case, immediately prompted revision would remain supported production, not independent transfer. A later independent opportunity would be needed to examine retention.

Proposed short activity:
1. Inspect. Show the applied facts, constraints and task together. Ask the learner to notice what is available, when and under what conditions; what participant needs are explicitly stated; and what is unknown. Keep the worked example out of this initial view so that the first response is not simply copying it. Reading or completing this step is not evidence of the capability.
2. Plan. Invite one editable response containing the proposed activity, the relevant resource and assistance arrangements, the supplied participant provisions, supporting facts, a fallback and any clarification needed. A compact prompt can use 'I propose ... because the case says ...; if ... changes, I would ... because ...; I still need to know ...'. This scaffold makes the intended reasoning visible but also makes the performance supported. Do not require an invented participant need or unnecessary clarification merely to fill a field. A learner may explain that the supplied facts resolve the relevant uncertainty.
3. Feedback. After the attempt, focus attention on a plan-to-fact connection that needs checking and explain why that connection matters. When a contradiction is actually established, feedback should identify the relevant supplied constraint, its consequence for the proposed action, and the issue the learner needs to revise. For example, using m00005's explicitly proposed changed case, a printer's physical availability is insufficient when its required operator is absent. This is a case-specific explanation, not a rule to carry into replacement cases. Accept the possibility of multiple justified plans; do not reward printer use as the desired answer. If the tool cannot establish whether an open response fits arbitrary replacement facts, it can still offer an honest reflection prompt: 'Which supplied fact supports this part of your plan? Is any required condition missing?' Such a prompt is instructional support, not a verified correctness judgment. A generic checklist alone must not be presented as evidence that the response was understood or validated.
4. Revise under a changed condition. For the starting fixture, m00005 supplies the change in Bea's availability. Invite the learner to state which dependency is affected, revise the affected action, and explain which other participant provisions still need to be maintained. A learner who initially chose the manual activity may reasonably retain it and explain why the changed printer assistance does not affect that plan. Requiring a visibly different answer would penalize that reasoning. Use the applied replacement scenario's own facts for subsequent cases; do not assume it contains a printer, the same permissions, or a viable manual alternative. If the change is unclear or contradictory, a specific clarification can be the appropriate response.

The proposed mechanism is repeated construction of an evidence-to-action explanation, followed by a focused opportunity to repair that explanation. Revealing a complete model plan before the learner's attempt would reduce the opportunity to observe their own construction. A worked example can be useful after an attempt or when explicitly requested, but a subsequent answer should then remain identified as supported. Skipping should allow the learner to inspect the case or leave practice without implying failure or completion of a learning objective. Resetting should allow a fresh attempt without generating a learning claim.

Evidence that could challenge the intended learning claim: a learner can name the assistance rule but still proposes the unsupported printer activity after the assistant is removed; a revision copies the suggested fallback without explaining its connection to available resources; a learner treats an unavailable resource as available in a different case despite success on the starting example; or a later unsupported attempt loses the plan-to-constraint reasoning. These observations would count against the specific claim being examined. An unexplained answer is insufficient evidence, rather than proof that the learner lacks the capability; difficulty understanding the prompt or expressing reasoning remains an alternative explanation to examine. Conversely, satisfaction, button clicks, completion and one prompted correct choice do not establish learning. Even a well-justified first answer shows performance and may reflect prior knowledge. A claim of improvement needs evidence beyond the existence of that answer.

Dependencies for the facilitator's next routing step: Assessment, Measurement, Evaluation should advise on a practical review method and the strength of claims warranted by baseline responses, supported revisions and any later transfer opportunity. Software Engineering should advise how the implemented interaction can keep each response and its feedback associated with the scenario actually applied, and make the support available at each attempt apparent; I am not specifying or certifying a technical solution. Learning Experience Design can advise whether the prompts and change/revision flow are understandable and manageable. Until the implemented bytes and those relevant decisions are available, my domain remains unapproved. No learner outcome or empirical effectiveness is asserted.

response.content:
Assessment-design proposal answering m00003, informed by the case proposal in m00005 and learning-design proposal in m00007. These are review criteria and inference limits, not an approval: no implemented version, observed learner response or evaluation result has been supplied.

Claim and task. The bounded capability to examine is whether a learner can construct and explain a plan whose material choices follow from the supplied facts and constraints, identify consequential uncertainty, and justify an available fallback or a clarification request when a dependency changes. A favored activity, fluent prose or completion of the interface does not establish this capability. The proposed task should ask for the plan and its reasons together, with the applied case available throughout. For arbitrary replacement cases, the target remains evidence-to-action reasoning; printer use, named people and the starting fixture's permissions are not universal criteria.

Observable criteria for review. Review the response against its actual applied case, using the following dimensions where relevant:
1. Resource fit: the proposed resources, quantities and capacity are supported by supplied facts, and the response explains any consequential limitation rather than assuming extra stock or places.
2. Time and assistance dependencies: the response connects a proposed action to the conditions required for it, including availability and operating permissions when the case supplies them. The reviewer should distinguish an action the case supports from one whose required condition is unknown or contradicted. Subject-Matter Expertise remains responsible for the workshop interpretation underlying any feasibility finding.
3. Stated participant provisions: the response connects the plan to the needs actually supplied, without presenting inferred needs or preferences as facts.
4. Contingency reasoning: a fallback has a stated trigger and is justified using resources and permissions available in that case; when no alternative is established, a focused clarification request can be appropriate. Naming an alternative without showing why it is available supplies incomplete evidence.
5. Response to change: the learner identifies the affected dependency and explains the resulting plan. Keeping an already feasible plan can demonstrate this reasoning if the learner explains why the changed condition does not affect it. A visibly different answer is not required.
6. Uncertainty: the learner identifies a material missing or conflicting fact and explains what decision depends on it, or explains why the supplied facts suffice for the bounded decision. Do not require an unnecessary uncertainty merely to fill a field.

Use criterion-level descriptions, not an invented numerical score or mastery threshold. A reviewer can record 'supported by the supplied evidence', 'explicit conflict with a supplied constraint', or 'insufficient evidence to judge', with the relevant response passage and case fact. Mark genuinely irrelevant dimensions as not applicable. Missing explanation can make reasoning unobservable even when the proposed action happens to be feasible; it is not by itself proof of an infeasible plan or inability. Conversely, polished reasoning cannot repair an explicitly contradicted operating condition. Do not average away such a conflict with credit for other dimensions. No inter-reviewer agreement or validated scoring interpretation exists yet.

Practical feedback for the first implementation. An open response to user-replaceable facts should not receive automatic correctness, feasibility or learning claims unless the implementation has a warranted way to establish the particular judgment. Presence of keywords, response length, mentioning every category or checking boxes cannot establish that the plan respects the case. A bounded tool can provide honest reflection support after submission: ask the learner to identify the fact supporting a resource or permission, check the dependency connecting an action to required assistance, and explain whether the fallback is available. Label this as guided self-review rather than a verified result. If a reviewer has actually established a contradiction, feedback should identify the response passage, the supplied constraint and the consequence to reconsider. For example, m00005 provides the case-specific basis for questioning printer use when its mandatory assistant is unavailable; that feedback must not be carried into an unrelated replacement scenario. Self-reported checklist completion is evidence of self-review activity, not independent confirmation of correctness.

Separate practice from assessment. Preserve the distinction between an initial response, feedback or examples shown, and a revision. The initial response in a scaffolded activity is still supported performance. A revision after a hint is evidence about performance with that support, not an independent assessment. Applying changed facts should make clear which case the next response addresses; old responses and feedback must not appear to evaluate the new case. Software Engineering should determine an appropriate technical method for associating each retained attempt with its applied scenario and the support available to it. This is an evidence requirement, not a prescribed implementation. Skip, reset, submission and self-review states should report actions taken, without claiming failure, mastery or learning.

Changed task and transfer. The proposed loss of Bea's assistance is a useful same-case adaptation opportunity. For a learner initially proposing printing, an informative revision explains the dependency failure and justifies an available alternative; for a learner initially proposing a manual activity, an informative response can explain why that activity remains supported. Neither response alone establishes transfer. To examine transfer support, use a separate fictional case with a meaningfully changed resource or support relationship, prepared or checked by Subject-Matter Expertise, and ask for a fresh plan and explanation before providing answer-specific hints or corrective feedback. Keep that case's facts visible. Apply the same reasoning criteria to the new facts, allowing different valid plans. Record whether support was requested or supplied, and describe any such result as supported performance. A small first implementation may remain explicitly a practice tool; it should not advertise an independent transfer measure unless that separate opportunity and review procedure actually exist.

Inference limits and alternative explanations. A successful first attempt may reflect prior knowledge. Improvement on the same task may reflect copying a hint, familiarity with the wording or remembering a model answer. A weak explanation may reflect difficulty understanding the prompt or expressing reasoning rather than inability to plan. Success on one closely similar changed case may depend on surface cues. These possibilities limit what the observations support. Human responses on a distinct task without answer-specific support would provide evidence about performance on that task; they would not by themselves establish durable retention, general workshop competence or a causal learning effect from the tool. A later independent opportunity would be needed to examine retention, and stronger evidence would be needed to attribute change to the tool. Synthetic responses and automated browser observations can examine interaction behavior and whether feedback is misleading; they cannot supply evidence of learning in people.

Dependencies and correction requests. Subject-Matter Expertise should check any case-specific feasibility interpretation and any distinct assessment fixture. Software Engineering should expose uncertainty honestly and prevent scenario replacement from inheriting old correctness judgments. If the proposed implementation uses a score, automatic feasibility label or transfer claim without the evidence described above, request correction before assessment approval. These are prospective review conditions, not allegations about an implementation that does not yet exist. My domain remains not reviewed until actual implemented bytes are available, and no learner outcome is asserted.

Interaction-design review answering m00013, based on the actual version 1 HTML supplied in m00015. The activity sequence is coherent for a small supported-practice candidate. The source describes a meaningful first attempt, honest reflection support, optional revision and a changed situation. I recommend one focused draft-preservation repair before learning-experience approval. This is a review of the supplied interface text and interaction definitions; I have not executed the artifact, observed learners or verified keyboard or assistive-technology behavior.

What each interaction offers the learner:

Inspect and plan. The applied facts, constraints and task are grouped together, with F and C references that a learner can use to explain a decision. The response area identifies its applied case. One editable response and an optional sentence scaffold let the learner construct a plan and its reasons without navigating a required form for every category. The wording permits a specific clarification request and explains that the learner need not invent uncertainty. Keeping a worked solution out of the initial view preserves an opportunity to construct an explanation. These are useful design provisions; their presence does not establish that a learner understands the case.

Self-review. After submission, the interface explicitly calls the material guided self-review and says the response has not been checked. Starting with one important action gives the learner a manageable point of entry: connect that action to a supplied fact, inspect a required condition, then consider the fallback and participant provisions where relevant. The additional prompts can support a broader review. Their wording is consistent with the boundaries proposed in m00007 and m00009. The tool supplies questions for the learner to use; it does not identify which part of the response is actually wrong. That limitation remains visible and should remain visible.

Revision and change. The previous submission is distinguished from the editable draft, and the text explains that another Try response action records a new submission. The supplied change creates a separately identified case and asks the learner to explain the affected dependency. It explicitly permits retaining a plan with reasons. That makes the interaction about reconsidering a decision rather than producing a visibly different answer. The previous response is available as optional starting text, while earlier responses and their case facts remain in history. The learner can therefore compare the original explanation with the changed situation without being required to rewrite everything. These provisions support the intended practice; no learning or transfer result follows from them.

Editing versus applying the scenario is explained clearly in the supplied interface. The editor has a separate heading, an explicit Apply scenario action and a message identifying unapplied changes. The applied case and response keep their case number. The invalid-input message says that the applied case and response remain unchanged, and Restore editor to applied case provides a recovery route. Applying different facts starts a separate response and labels older records with their original case. Those are the right interaction requirements for preventing an editor draft from being mistaken for the facts being answered. Actual state transitions remain for Software Engineering to verify.

Skip and reset also have distinct stated purposes. Skip preserves the draft and records, permits continued inspection, and changes Revise response to Resume practice. Reset is described as clearing every response draft and the history while retaining the applied case and unapplied scenario edits. Neither action assigns a learning judgment. The labels and help text provide a usable explanation of these choices. Explicit text labels, ordinary text entry, native buttons and visible focus styling provide an appropriate implementation basis for keyboard access; I cannot certify accessibility from this source review.

Focused repair for Software Engineering: protect a current draft when the learner reuses earlier text. In version 1, the Copy previous response into this draft control remains enabled whenever practice is not skipped, including after the learner has written a new draft.
